paras.text: Let us consider buta-1,3-diene to illustrate the phenomenon of conjugation. All the four carbon atoms in buta-1,3-diene are sp²-hybridized. The C–C and C–H sigma bonds are the result of the overlap of sp²-hybrid orbitals with each other and with 1s orbitals of the hydrogen atoms respectively. All the carbon and hydrogen atoms lie in the same plane. Additionally, each of the four carbon atom also possess an unhybridized p orbital, which are perpendicular to the plane of sigma bonds. These four p orbitals overlap to form delocalized pi molecular orbitals (Figure.16.4). These delocalized pi electrons are thus attracted by all four carbon atoms. The delocalization of pi electrons is responsible for greater stability of buta-1,3-diene. As a consequence of conjugation, the C–C single bond in buta-1,3-diene is 148 pm (1.48 Å) which is shorter than the normal C–C single bonds (154 pm) of alkane while the C–C double bond are 137 pm (1.37 Å) which are longer than normal isolated C–C double bonds (134 pm).

When the double bonds in a diene are separated from each other by two or more single bonds, they are called isolated double bonds. Adjacent double bonds in a diene are referred as comulated double bonds.

16.5.4 Relative Stability of Alkenes

Various alkenes have different stability which depends upon the position of the double bond in the molecule and the number, nature and relative position of substituents on double bonded carbon atoms. In general, the greater the number of alkyl groups attached to the double bonded carbons, the greater is the stability of alkene. For geometric isomers of an alkene, trans-isomer is always more stable than cis-isomers (Section 16.6.2.1). For isomeric dienes, conjugated dienes are more stable than non-conjugated.

Measurement and comparison of the heats of hydrogenation or heats of combustion of different isomeric alkenes, give us a clue about the relative stability of these alkenes. Stable alkenes evolve small amount of heat upon combustion and hydrogenation and vice versa.

Consider the heats of combustion of the four isomeric butylenes of molecular formula C₄H₈, as given below. Comparison of the heats of combustion of butylenes shows that but-1-ene evolves the largest amount of heat on combustion. In other words, but-1-ene possess the highest energy and is thus the least stable of the four butylenes. Similarly isobutylene (2-methylpropene) has lowest value of enthalpy of combustion, and the most stable of the four isomers.

16.5.5 Preparation of Alkenes

Alkenes can be prepared by the following methods.

16.5.5.1 Dehydration of Alcohols

When an alcohol is heated at 170°C, in the presence of sulfuric acid, a water molecule is eliminated, resulting in the formation of an alkene.

Let us consider buta-1,3-diene to illustrate the phenomenon of conjugation. All the four carbon atoms in buta-1,3-diene are sp²-hybridized. The C–C and C–H sigma bonds are the result of the overlap of sp²-hybrid orbitals with each other and with 1s orbitals of the hydrogen atoms respectively. All the carbon and hydrogen atoms lie in the same plane. Additionally, each of the four carbon atom also possess an unhybridized p orbital, which are perpendicular to the plane of sigma bonds. These four p orbitals overlap to form delocalized pi molecular orbitals (Figure.16.4). These delocalized pi electrons are thus attracted by all four carbon atoms. The delocalization of pi electrons is responsible for greater stability of buta-1,3-diene. As a consequence of conjugation, the C–C single bond in buta-1,3-diene is 148 pm (1.48 Å) which is shorter than the normal C–C single bonds (154 pm) of alkane while the C–C double bond are 137 pm (1.37 Å) which are longer than normal isolated C–C double bonds (134 pm).

Tidbit

When the double bonds in a diene are separated from each other by two or more single bonds, they are called isolated double bonds. Adjacent double bonds in a diene are referred as comulated double bonds.

Figure 16.4 Overlap of four p orbitals in buta-1,3-diene.

16.5.4 Relative Stability of Alkenes

Various alkenes have different stability which depends upon the position of the double bond in the molecule and the number, nature and relative position of substituents on double bonded carbon atoms. In general, the greater the number of alkyl groups attached to the double bonded carbons, the greater is the stability of alkene. For geometric isomers of an alkene, trans-isomer is always more stable than cis-isomers (Section 16.6.2.1). For isomeric dienes, conjugated dienes are more stable than non-conjugated.

Measurement and comparison of the heats of hydrogenation or heats of combustion of different isomeric alkenes, give us a clue about the relative stability of these alkenes. Stable alkenes evolve small amount of heat upon combustion and hydrogenation and vice versa.

Consider the heats of combustion of the four isomeric butylenes of molecular formula C₄H₈, as given below. Comparison of the heats of combustion of butylenes shows that but-1-ene evolves the largest amount of heat on combustion. In other words, but-1-ene possess the highest energy and is thus the least stable of the four butylenes. Similarly isobutylene (2-methylpropene) has lowest value of enthalpy of combustion, and the most stable of the four isomers.

16.5.5 Preparation of Alkenes

Alkenes can be prepared by the following methods.

16.5.5.1 Dehydration of Alcohols

When an alcohol is heated at 170°C, in the presence of sulfuric acid, a water molecule is eliminated, resulting in the formation of an alkene.
